title: THE MAN JESUS MADE THE HERO WAS THE MAN EVERYONE LEAST EXPECTED
paragraphs: THE MAN JESUS MADE THE HERO WAS THE MAN EVERYONE LEAST EXPECTED

Why did Jesus choose a despised Samaritan to expose the danger of religious pride? The shocking truth behind Luke 10:25–37 might change how you see your neighbor, your faith, and the mercy that rescued your own soul.
What if the person you have spent your life looking down on is the very person Jesus would use to teach you what loving God actually looks like?
That question should make us uncomfortable.
Because somewhere along the road between knowing Scripture and actually living it, something can go terribly wrong.
You can memorize Bible verses and still have a heart that refuses to love.
You can attend church every Sunday and still walk past someone who desperately needs mercy.
You can defend the truth with your mouth while denying its transforming power through your actions.
And perhaps the most frightening possibility of all?
You can be so certain that you are standing on the right side of religion that you never notice the wounded person lying at your feet.
Jesus knew exactly how to expose that danger.
And He did it by making the wrong man the hero.
At least, the wrong man in the eyes of His audience.
A Samaritan.
Someone many of His Jewish listeners would have been conditioned to distrust, avoid, or regard as religiously compromised.
But before we reach the Samaritan, we need to meet the man whose question started everything.
Because his question sounds remarkably like something we might ask today.
And the answer Jesus gave was far more unsettling than he expected.
Luke 10:25 tells us that a lawyer stood up to test Jesus.
Not a lawyer in the modern courtroom sense, but an expert in the Law of Moses. Someone trained to understand, interpret, and discuss the commandments of God.
He asked Jesus, “Teacher, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?” (Luke 10:25, KJV).
Notice the tension already present.
He is asking about eternal life, but Luke tells us he is testing Jesus.
He knows religious language. He understands theological questions. He has studied the commandments.
Yet knowing the right questions is not the same as having a surrendered heart.
Jesus responds by asking what is written in the Law and how the man reads it.
The lawyer answers correctly.
Love the Lord your God with all your heart, soul, strength, and mind, and love your neighbor as yourself.
He draws from Deuteronomy 6:5 and Leviticus 19:18.
In Hebrew, the opening command of Deuteronomy 6:5 begins:
וְאָהַבְתָּ אֵת יְהוָה אֱלֹהֶיךָ
Ve'ahavta et Adonai Elohekha.
“And you shall love the LORD your God.”
Here, Adonai is the traditional Jewish reverential reading of the divine name written in the Hebrew text.
The command is not simply to acknowledge God's existence, admire His teachings, or perform religious duties.
It calls for wholehearted love.
Not a compartment of your life.
Not your Sunday mornings alone.
Your heart. Your soul. Your strength.
Everything.
And the second command, from Leviticus 19:18, reaches beyond private devotion into the way we treat other people.
וְאָהַבְתָּ לְרֵעֲךָ כָּמוֹךָ
Ve'ahavta lere'akha kamokha.
“And you shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
The lawyer knows these words.
Jesus even tells him that he has answered correctly.
But then Luke records a detail that changes the entire conversation.
“But he, willing to justify himself, said unto Jesus, And who is my neighbour?” (Luke 10:29, KJV).
There it is.
The question beneath the question.
He wants to know where the obligation ends.
Who qualifies?
Who deserves my concern?
How far must my compassion extend before I can consider myself obedient?
And that is where this ancient conversation becomes painfully modern.
Because we may not ask, “Who is my neighbor?” in exactly those words.
But we ask it in other ways.
Do I really have to forgive someone who hurt me?
Must I show kindness to someone who disagrees with everything I believe?
Should I care about people who would never care about me?
Why should I help someone whose problems seem to be the consequences of their own choices?
What about the person who embarrassed me?
The family member who betrayed my trust?
The stranger whose life looks nothing like mine?
We may never say it aloud, but sometimes our hearts whisper:
Lord, surely You don't expect me to love that person.
Jesus answers with a story.
And the road He chooses is not an accident.
A man is traveling from Jerusalem down to Jericho.
The journey descends through rugged terrain. In the ancient world, stretches of that road could leave travelers vulnerable to attack.
The man falls among robbers.
They strip him.
Beat him.
Take what they want.
And leave him half dead.
Try to imagine the scene without rushing ahead to the familiar ending.
A body lying in the dust.
Clothing torn away.
Blood on the ground.
A man who had plans when he left Jerusalem, who perhaps had family expecting him, who never imagined that an ordinary journey would end with him fighting to remain conscious.
We are not told his name.
We are not told his occupation.
We are not told his moral history.
Jesus does not tell us whether he was wealthy or poor, wise or foolish, respected or despised.
And that omission matters.
The wounded man does not arrive with a résumé proving that he deserves compassion.
He simply needs mercy.
Then footsteps approach.
A priest.
Someone associated with worship, sacrifice, and the sacred responsibilities of Israel.
Surely he will stop.
Surely a man familiar with the commandments of God will recognize what love requires.
But Jesus says that when the priest sees the wounded man, he passes by on the other side.
Another traveler approaches.
A Levite.
Another man connected with the religious life of Israel.
He sees the wounded man too.
And he also passes by.
Notice what Jesus does not tell us.
He does not explain their motives.
He does not say they were afraid of ritual impurity.
He does not say they were late for religious duties.
He does not tell us whether they feared robbers were still nearby.
Those explanations may sound plausible, but the text does not give them.
What the text does tell us is enough.
They saw him.
And they passed by.
That is the part that should trouble us.
Because sometimes the most revealing moment in our spiritual lives is not what we say when everyone is listening.
It is what we do when someone else's suffering interrupts our plans.
We see the exhausted mother barely holding her family together.
We notice the elderly neighbor who has become invisible.
We know the brother or sister in Christ who has stopped attending church.
We hear about the struggling family.
We recognize the person who has been publicly humiliated.
And we tell ourselves we will pray.
We tell ourselves someone else is better equipped.
We tell ourselves we are too busy.
Prayer is precious. It is commanded and necessary.
But prayer must never become an excuse for withholding the practical love we are able to give.
First John 3:17 asks how God's love abides in someone who possesses material resources, sees a brother or sister in need, and closes their heart.
That is not a condemnation of every person who cannot help everyone.
Our resources, responsibilities, and capacities are limited.
But it is a serious warning against using religious words to conceal a refusal to care.
And then Jesus introduces the third traveler.
A Samaritan.
To modern readers, that word may sound harmless because we already know the expression “Good Samaritan.”
But Jesus' original listeners did not hear it that way.
Jews and Samaritans had a long history of religious conflict, competing claims about sacred worship, and mutual hostility.
The Samaritans identified with Israel's heritage but worshiped at Mount Gerizim rather than accepting Jerusalem as the exclusive center of worship. The division had deep historical roots.
John 4:9 directly acknowledges the strained relationship between Jews and Samaritans.
Jesus is not merely introducing a man from another town.
He is placing a socially and religiously unwelcome outsider in the position where His listeners might have expected a respected member of their own community.
And then comes the turning point.
Luke 10:33 says:
“But a certain Samaritan, as he journeyed, came where he was: and when he saw him, he had compassion on him.” (KJV).
The Greek word translated “had compassion” is:
ἐσπλαγχνίσθη
Esplanchnisthē.
It comes from the verb splagchnizomai, expressing deep, inward compassion.
Not casual sympathy.
Not distant pity.
Not the polite sadness we feel before continuing with our own lives.
It describes compassion that reaches deeply within a person.
And in this story, that compassion does not remain an emotion.
It becomes action.
The Samaritan approaches the wounded man.
He treats his injuries with oil and wine, and binds his wounds.
He places him on his own animal.
He takes him to an inn.
He cares for him.
The next day, he gives the innkeeper two denarii and promises to reimburse additional necessary expenses when he returns.
A denarius was commonly associated with a day's wage for a laborer in the first-century world.
The Samaritan's care costs him something.
Time.
Resources.
Comfort.
Personal involvement.
He does not merely feel sorry for the man.
He allows another person's suffering to change his plans.
And perhaps this is where the story begins to find us.
Because compassion is easy to admire when it costs us nothing.
It becomes much harder when it requires patience with someone who has wounded our pride.
When it requires listening to someone whose pain we cannot quickly fix.
When it requires helping without expecting applause.
When it requires giving generously without using generosity to control another person.
When it requires refusing to turn another person's humiliation into entertainment.
When it requires seeing the humanity of someone we have already placed into a category.
And that last one may be the most uncomfortable of all.
Because the Samaritan did not need the wounded man to become like him before he offered help.
He did not demand agreement before showing compassion.
He did not investigate whether the man had earned his suffering.
He did not ask whether helping would improve his reputation.
He saw a human being in need.
And he acted mercifully.
Now consider what Jesus does next.
He turns back to the lawyer.
But He does not answer the original question in the form the lawyer expected.
The lawyer asked, “Who is my neighbor?”
Jesus asks which of the three travelers became a neighbor to the wounded man.
The Greek of Luke 10:36 includes the phrase:
πλησίον δοκεῖ σοι γεγονέναι
Plēsion dokei soi gegonenai.
The sense is, “seems to you to have become a neighbor.”
The emphasis is striking.
The lawyer wanted to identify the boundaries of the people he was obligated to love.
Jesus directs his attention toward becoming the kind of person who shows mercy.
The lawyer responds:
“The one who showed him mercy.”
Then Jesus says:
“Go, and do thou likewise.” (Luke 10:37, KJV).
And suddenly the question is no longer safely theoretical.
It has become personal.
Not simply, Who qualifies for my love?
But, Am I becoming a neighbor to someone who needs it?
Not, How little compassion can I offer and still satisfy the commandment?
But, What would love require of me here?
This is why Jesus made the Samaritan the hero.
He was exposing the danger of assuming that religious status automatically proves obedience to God.
He was dismantling the idea that compassion should stop at the borders of our preferred community.
He was confronting the human tendency to make love conditional upon familiarity, approval, or shared identity.
And He was showing that mercy can appear where religious prejudice has taught us not to expect it.
But there is something else we must not miss.
Jesus was not teaching that the priest and Levite were evil because they were Jewish, or that the Samaritan was righteous merely because he belonged to another group.
Jesus Himself was Jewish.
His disciples were Jewish.
The Law that commanded love of neighbor belonged to Israel's Scriptures.
The point is not that one ethnic group is morally superior to another.
The point is that the true demands of God's commandment cannot be satisfied by religious identity alone.
The Samaritan becomes the moral example because he acts with mercy.
And that should humble every one of us.
Especially those of us who call ourselves followers of Jesus.
Because Christianity is not a badge that makes us better than our neighbors.
It is a confession that we need the grace of God.
And that grace should change how we treat people.
But now we must go deeper.
Because if we stop here, we may turn the parable into nothing more than a motivational speech about kindness.
Be compassionate.
Help strangers.
Treat people better.
All true.
All necessary.
But Luke's Gospel gives us a much greater horizon.
Remember how this conversation began.
“What shall I do to inherit eternal life?”
The lawyer knows the commandment.
Love God completely.
Love your neighbor as yourself.
Jesus affirms the righteousness of that command.
But when we measure our own lives against such wholehearted love, a painful truth emerges.
Who among us has loved God with every thought, every desire, every decision, and every moment?
Who has consistently loved every neighbor with the same concern we naturally have for ourselves?
Who has never withheld mercy?
Never entertained contempt?
Never chosen convenience over compassion?
Never protected pride at the expense of love?
If eternal life depended on our flawless performance of these commandments, none of us could stand before God claiming perfect obedience.
Romans 3:23 declares that all have sinned and fall short of God's glory.
And Romans 3:24 announces the breathtaking answer: sinners are justified by God's grace as a gift through the redemption found in Christ Jesus.
The Law reveals the holiness of God's will.
The Gospel reveals the Savior who rescues sinners who cannot make themselves righteous.
And this is where the story becomes more than a mirror exposing our failures.
It becomes an invitation to the grace that can transform us.
We should be careful here.
Jesus does not explicitly identify Himself as the Samaritan in Luke 10.
The primary meaning of the parable is the command to show mercy across human boundaries.
But Christians throughout history have also reflected on how the Samaritan's costly compassion can remind us of the greater mercy revealed in Christ.
That is a theological reflection, not a replacement for the parable's original meaning.
And what a beautiful reflection it is.
Because the Gospel tells us that Jesus did not wait for sinners to make themselves worthy before He came to save them.
Romans 5:8 declares that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Think about that.
Before you knew how to pray eloquently.
Before you understood every doctrine.
Before you cleaned up your reputation.
Before you could explain the mess you had made.
Before you knew how to stop pretending.
Christ loved sinners.
Not because sin was harmless.
Not because rebellion did not matter.
But because His mercy is greater than the ruin we cannot repair ourselves.
At the cross, Jesus did not minimize evil.
He bore the judgment our sins deserve.
And through His resurrection, He opened the way to forgiveness, reconciliation with God, and new life.
The Samaritan paid money to help a wounded traveler recover.
Jesus gave His life to redeem sinners.
The Samaritan carried a wounded man to safety.
Jesus calls the weary and burdened to come to Him.
The Samaritan promised to return and settle an outstanding cost.
Jesus accomplished the saving work that no human effort could complete.
The comparison has its limits, but it points us toward a glorious truth.
The mercy Jesus commands is the kind of mercy we ourselves desperately need from Him.
And maybe that is the part of this story you were not expecting.
Because perhaps you have spent years identifying with the people who walk past.
You remember the times you should have stopped.
The apology you refused to make.
The hungry person you ignored.
The relationship you allowed bitterness to poison.
The wounded believer you judged without hearing their story.
And you wonder whether your failures have finally made you unworthy of God's love.
Listen carefully.
Your sin is serious.
But the answer is not to hide it beneath more religious performance.
The answer is to bring it into the light before Jesus Christ.
Repentance is not pretending the past did not happen.
It is turning from sin toward the Savior.
First John 1:9 teaches that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
That promise is not permission to continue in unrepentant cruelty.
It is an invitation to stop running from the One who can change us.
And perhaps someone else reading this identifies with the man lying on the road.
Not because your circumstances are identical, but because you know what it feels like to be abandoned.
To be hurt and then blamed for being wounded.
To watch people who speak beautifully about love disappear when loving you becomes inconvenient.
To be passed over by people you thought would protect you.
Maybe your suffering came from someone who knew Scripture.
Maybe you were humiliated by someone who carried a Bible.
Maybe you trusted a spiritual leader who failed you.
And now even the language of faith brings back painful memories.
If that is your story, please hear this distinction.
The failure of someone who claims to represent Jesus is not the character of Jesus Himself.
He does not approve of religious hypocrisy.
He confronted it.
He does not command us to ignore injustice.
He calls us to truth and righteousness.
He does not require you to return to an unsafe situation to prove that you have forgiven someone.
Forgiveness does not erase accountability, and showing mercy does not mean enabling abuse.
You can seek healing, establish necessary boundaries, pursue justice, and still refuse to surrender your heart to hatred.
Jesus understands betrayal.
He understands rejection.
He understands suffering at the hands of sinful people.
And He remains the Savior who welcomes the weary.
But whether you recognize yourself in the wounded man, the passing travelers, or the person struggling to learn compassion, the invitation of Christ is the same.
Come to Him.
Not with a polished performance.
Not with a rehearsed explanation.
Come honestly.
And let His grace do more than comfort you.
Let it change you.
Because the Gospel does not merely forgive the person you used to be.
It begins transforming the person you are becoming.
Ephesians 2:8–10 holds both truths together.
We are saved by grace through faith, not by works that allow us to boast.
And we are created in Christ Jesus for good works that God prepared for us to walk in.
Do you see the order?
We do not earn salvation by becoming impressive Samaritans.
We receive salvation through Jesus Christ.
Then His grace teaches us to walk in the love He commands.
Our good works are not the price of God's acceptance.
They are the fruit of His transforming grace.
That distinction matters more than we sometimes realize.
Because without grace, the parable can leave us crushed beneath a command we have repeatedly failed to fulfill.
But without obedience, we can turn grace into an excuse for a faith that never changes how we treat anyone.
The Gospel rejects both errors.
Jesus saves us by grace.
And the Jesus who saves us calls us to follow Him.
So the next time you see someone hurting, remember the road to Jericho.
Remember that the priest saw.
The Levite saw.
The Samaritan saw.
But only one allowed compassion to become costly action.
And ask yourself a question that may be harder than any theological argument you have ever won.
What would it look like for me to love this person in a way that honors Jesus?
Perhaps it means offering practical help.
Perhaps it means listening instead of assuming.
Perhaps it means making a phone call you have delayed.
Perhaps it means refusing to spread a rumor.
Perhaps it means feeding someone who is hungry.
Perhaps it means asking forgiveness.
Perhaps it means welcoming a person your social circle has quietly decided to reject.
Or perhaps it means recognizing that you cannot carry every burden alone, and helping someone find the appropriate support they need.
Love is not always dramatic.
Sometimes it is quiet.
Sometimes nobody applauds.
Sometimes the person you help cannot repay you.
Sometimes compassion looks like remaining present when everyone else has already left.
And sometimes it begins with admitting that your own heart has grown colder than you wanted to believe.
That is not a reason to despair.
It is a reason to return to Christ.
Because Jesus did not tell this parable merely to produce a moment of religious embarrassment.
He called His listener to a different way of living.
“Go, and do thou likewise.”
Those words still stand.
And they confront something deeply personal.
We often want Jesus to confirm that we are already the good people in the story.
But He loves us too much to leave our assumptions unchallenged.
He may show us that we have been walking past people we were called to love.
He may expose prejudices we have dressed up as discernment.
He may reveal how easily we confuse biblical knowledge with spiritual maturity.
And He may use the very person we have dismissed to teach us what mercy looks like.
That is uncomfortable grace.
Grace that does not flatter us.
Grace that tells the truth.
Grace that leads us to repentance.
Grace that begins rewriting a story we thought was already finished.
And that is why this message belongs at the heart of Gospel Warrior.
The scandal is that the religiously respected travelers failed to show mercy while the despised outsider became the example.
The grace is that Jesus does not leave us imprisoned in our failures, prejudices, or self-righteousness.
He calls us to Himself.
He forgives repentant sinners.
He gives new life.
And by His Spirit, He forms in us the kind of love that no amount of religious appearance can manufacture.
Maybe today you need to stop defending your coldness.
Maybe you need to stop allowing someone else's failures to define the character of God.
Maybe you need to stop trying to earn the forgiveness that Christ offers through His finished work.
Or maybe you need to take the first small, costly step toward loving a neighbor you have been avoiding.
Whatever the Holy Spirit is bringing to your attention through Scripture, do not bury it beneath another scroll, another distraction, or another religious excuse.
Bring it before Jesus.
And respond to Him.
Someone else may need to hear that repentance, forgiveness, and transformation are possible.
You do not need to reveal private wounds publicly to prove your faith. But honest testimony can encourage another person who thought they were struggling alone.
And please, think of one person who needs to encounter this message.
Not someone you want to shame.
Someone you genuinely want to encourage.
There is also a deeper way to stand with this ministry.
Every article, every biblical resource, every opportunity to reach another person with the message of Christ represents work that needs faithful stewardship and practical support.
It does not purchase salvation, forgiveness, spiritual status, or a greater claim upon God's blessing.
And it should never replace your responsibility to care for your household or your thoughtful giving to your local church.
Second Corinthians 9:7 reminds us that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
That is the spirit in which we invite you.
Not pressure.
Not guilt.
But an opportunity to participate in something you believe is worth supporting.
If you want to glorify God through generosity, supporting faithful Gospel ministry can be one meaningful way to do that, alongside the many other acts of love and obedience He calls us to practice.
These products can be meaningful reminders of faith, opportunities for conversations about Jesus, and thoughtful gifts for people you love.
It is the opportunity to support a continuing work of discipleship.
Those resources are an invitation to keep learning, keep examining the Scriptures, and keep growing in your walk with Christ.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Share the Gospel.
Encourage someone.
Show mercy.
And His grace is never for sale.
Before you leave this story, though, there is one final question.
What if tomorrow you find yourself on that road?
Not literally between Jerusalem and Jericho.
But in an ordinary moment when another person's suffering crosses your path.
You have somewhere to go.
Something important to finish.
A schedule to protect.
A reason not to get involved.
And then you see someone who needs mercy.
Nobody is recording.
Nobody is waiting to congratulate you.
Nobody will know whether you stopped or walked away.
Except God.
What will you do?
The answer may reveal more about the direction of your discipleship than a thousand declarations about how much you love Jesus.
Because the Samaritan did not become the hero of the parable by announcing that he was compassionate.
He became the example by showing mercy.
And the lawyer who wanted to justify himself was left with a command that could no longer be reduced to an argument.
“Go, and do thou likewise.”
May we never become so proud of knowing the Bible that we forget to obey the Lord who gave it.
May we never become so protective of our religious reputation that we abandon the people God calls us to love.
And may we never forget that the mercy we extend to others is a response to the immeasurably greater mercy we have received through Jesus Christ.
Because one day, when all our arguments have gone silent and every earthly title has faded, what will matter is not how successfully we appeared righteous before other people.
What will matter is whether we truly belonged to Christ—the Savior whose grace forgives, whose Spirit transforms, and whose love teaches His people to walk in mercy.
The most heartbreaking thing about the road to Jericho was not that two religious men failed to see a wounded stranger. It was that they saw him—and kept walking.
